                    ### Question
                    A 12-year-old boy is brought in by his mother with a 2-day history of fever and generalized weakness. She says that her son was involved in a school fight with some other kids 4 days ago and sustained minor injuries to the face. He was otherwise well, until this morning, when he complained of pain in his right eye. Physical examination reveals periorbital erythema and edema of the right eye, along with ophthalmoplegia and proptosis. Which of the following findings will most likely be present in this patient on the affected side as a sequela of his current condition?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Anesthesia along the CN V3 distribution
opb. Decreased vision with sparing of the optic disc
opc. Monocular diplopia
opd. Intact sympathetic innervation to the pupil, but not parasympathetic innervation
ope. Absent blink reflex

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The 12-year-old boy's presentation of fever, weakness, periorbital erythema, edema, ophthalmoplegia, and proptosis suggests orbital cellulitis, likely due to the recent facial injuries. In orbital cellulitis, cranial nerve involvement is common, particularly affecting the oculomotor nerve (CN III), which can lead to ophthalmoplegia and potentially affect sensory pathways. The most likely sequela on the affected side would be anesthesia along the CN V3 distribution due to possible involvement of the trigeminal nerve. Other options like decreased vision, monocular diplopia, and absent blink reflex may occur but are less directly supported by the clinical picture. Intact sympathetic innervation is unlikely due to the involvement of cranial nerves. Therefore, the best-supported finding is anesthesia along the CN V3 distribution.
